Simultaneous Optimization of Electric Ferry
Operations and Charging Infrastructure
Juan Pablo Bertucci1, Theo Hofman1, Mauro Salazar1
Abstract—Electrification of marine transport is a promising
solution to reduce sector greenhouse gas emissions and opera-
tional costs. However, the large upfront cost of electric vessels
and the required charging infrastructure can be a barrier to
the development of this technology. Optimization algorithms that
jointly design the charging infrastructure and the operation of
electric vessels can help to reduce these costs and make these
projects viable. In this paper, we present a mixed-integer linear
programming optimization framework that jointly schedules
ferry operations, charging infrastructure and ship battery size.
We analyze our algorithms with the case of the China Zorrilla,
the largest electric ferry in the world, which will operate between
Buenos Aires and Colonia del Sacramento in 2025. We find that
the joint system and operations design can reduce the total costs
by 7.8% compared to a scenario with fixed power limits and no
port energy management system.
I. INTRODUCTION
Maritime electrification is gaining traction due to its poten-
tial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and lower operational
costs [1], [2]. Recent deployments of battery-electric ferries
on short- to medium-range routes have demonstrated their
technical and economic viability. Notable examples include
Denmark’sEllen[3] and Norway’sMF Ampere[4], where
high-capacity battery systems and rapid-charging infrastruc-
ture enabled fully electric, zero-emission operations. Similar
benefits were observed in retrofitting existing vessels, such
as the Swedish-Danish ferriesTycho BraheandAurora[5],
which achieved significant reductions in operating costs. Addi-
tionally, the upcoming deployment of the largest fully electric
ferryChina Zorrillain the R ´ıo de la Plata in late 2025 further
supports the trend toward maritime electrification. However,
broader implementation of electric ferries is limited by the
high upfront investments and substantial power infrastructure
requirements, as well as the technichal limitations of range.
Traditionally, infrastructure sizing and ferry operations are
optimized separately, neglecting their interdependencies. This
fragmented approach can lead to oversized infrastructure,
operational inefficiencies, and higher costs.
Related literature:This work relates to two main research
streams: optimal all-electric ferry operations and optimized
charging infrastructures. The first stream focuses on energy
management and power dispatch on the vessel side. Ge-
netic algorithms have been used to balance economic and
environmental scheduling [6], while nonlinear optimization
formulations have been proposed for comparative analysis

economic analyses were developed in [11] finding the route

in [12] show savings in operational costs, while case studies
validate cost competitiveness of electrification under realistic
load profiles [13], [14]. The second stream addresses charging
logistics and port-side infrastructure. Research has examined
cold ironing and onshore battery systems to navigate grid
limitations and reduce emissions for short-berthing ships [15],
with additional work detailing system designs and perfor-
mance for high-power demands [16]. Life-cycle cost mod-
els inform optimal sizing of local renewable generation and
storage [17]. Using storage for grid support in trasnportation
charging infrastructure applications has been recognized as key
to decrease costs in other transportation domains [18]. Despite
these advancements, the literature still lacks a comprehensive
methodology that addresses large-capacity, high-speed ferry
operations simultaneously accounting for long-term battery
degradation, and shore-side charging infrastructure design with
global optimality guarantees.
Statement of Contributions:To address this gap, this paper
introduces a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) op-
timization framework that simultaneously determines optimal
ferry scheduling, battery sizing, and port-side charging infras-
tructure design. The proposed method guarantees globally op-
timal solutions and explicitly integrates operational constraints
with infrastructure investment decisions.

F . Discussion
A few comments are in order. First, the study assumes
that vessel displacement varies only slightly with changes in
battery configuration. This simplification aids in the modeling
process but may warrant further investigation in cases where
battery sizing significantly affects the vessel’s weight distri-
bution. Second, the MILP scalability to a large fleet of ves-
sels is limited. Future research should explore decomposition
methods or alternative solution strategies that can handle larger
fleet sizes more efficiently. Finally, extending the framework to
incorporate Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) services is straightforward.
However, such an extension was omitted from this paper due
to the absence of detailed turnaround times and the lack of
established incentive structures in the case study markets.
III. CASESTUDY
In this section we describe the input parameters and exper-
iments conducted to test the optimization algorithm. . We use
the data for the CZ, assuming a future service of two ferries
working to cover all the current demand between Colonia
(CO) and Buenos Aires (BA), as illustrated in Fig. 2. The
vessel is planned to have capacity for 2100 passengers and
225 vehicles. The catamaran twin hulls are mostly aluminium,
with a total length of 130m, beam of 32m and draft of
3.5m. The total battery capacity will be 40 MWh, powered
by 8 axis electric motors, optimized for speeds of 25kn.

IV. RESULTS
In this section we provide our results for our four exper-
iments. Experiment 1 corresponds to the expected design of
the project. Experiment 2 shows the resulting design allowing
for PV generation and an optimized peak power. Experiment
3 includes adds the possibility of a stationary battery. Experi-
ment 4 additionally allows for optimized vessel battery design.
The final designs and resulting costs are given in II. Table II
summarizes the resulting designs and costs. Then we describe
the vessel results in Fig. 3, and then the shore-side results in
Fig. 4 under the cost optimal solution (Experiment 4).
A. Designs and Costs
Experiment 1 represents the current design, without local
EMS or PV generation. This configuration incurs the highest
energy and infrastructure costs and an overall cost of $184,370.
In Experiment 2, a maximum 2.5MW PV system is introduced
at each port. This addition results in a total cost reduction of
$14,720, driven by reduced energy costs. This is due to the
reduced energy purchased () from the grid and extra revenue
produced (). In all the remaining cases the final PV design was

B. Vessel Results
Figure 3 presents the operation curves for experiment 4.
The figure illustrates the energy stateE vand power exchanges
for each vessel. Grey regions indicate mooring periods during
which vessels can charge. The energyE vexhibits a cyclic
pattern aligned with mooring periods, with frequent charging
events that bring the state-of-charge close to its upper bound.
The dominant power source is the grid (P g2v), whereas the
battery-to-vessel (P b2v) and PV-to-vessel (P pv2v) flows are
comparatively smaller and used during sunlight hours.
C. Port Side Results
Figure 4 presents the energy and power dynamics at both
ports. We observe the grid-to-vessel powerP g2vdominates,
indicating a high dependence on the grid for direct vessel
charging at both ports. Nevertheless, the battery-to-vessel
powerP b2vis also utilized frequently, suggesting the bat-
tery is actively supporting charging. Photovoltaic generation
Ppvis limited and concentrated during daytime, contributing
marginally to the overall power demand. Grid-to-batteryP g2b
and battery-to-gridP b2gflows are present but less frequent,
suggesting the battery is primarily used for local vessel support
rather than energy arbitrage.
V. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we present an optimization framework aimed
at improving the economic viability of electric-powered ship
services by jointly optimizing charging schedules, infrastruc-
ture investments, and speed profiles. Compared to an unopti-
mized scenario—with fixed maximum power station capacity
and predetermined schedules based on planned itineraries—
our method reduces total costs (comprising both capital and

operational expenditures) by 7.8%. The proposed optimiza-
tion framework not only serves as a design planning tool
but also as an operational platform for weekly scheduling.
Future work will extend this study by incorporating power
consumption variability along the route, moving beyond the
current simplified modeling approach. Additionally, we plan
to integrate stochastic forecasts for weather and prices, as well
as a more detailed treatment of battery degradation. All results

Overall, our results with conservative price values confirm that

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) optimization framework designed to simultaneously optimize electric ferry operations and charging infrastructure. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Statement:** The electrification of marine transport, particularly ferries, offers significant environmental and cost benefits but is hindered by high upfront costs for vessels and charging infrastructure. Traditional separate optimization of infrastructure and operations leads to inefficiencies and higher costs.
*   **Proposed Solution:** The paper introduces an MILP framework that jointly optimizes ferry scheduling, battery sizing, and port-side charging infrastructure design to achieve global optimality and reduce overall costs.
*   **Methodology:** The document details the MILP formulation, including definitions of sets, decision variables, and constraints.
    *   **Decision Variables:** These include port-side energy system parameters (peak grid connection, PV generation, battery storage capacity and power), vessel battery size, vessel energy state, charging power, and vessel operational variables like travel time and speed.
    *   **Constraints:** The framework incorporates vessel operational constraints (departure/arrival times, travel time, energy consumption, battery state of charge limits, charging power limits) and shore-side constraints (power flow from grid, PV, and batteries).
*   **Case Study:** The proposed algorithm is analyzed using the case of the "China Zorrilla," a large electric ferry operating between Buenos Aires and Colonia del Sacramento.
*   **Key Findings:** The joint optimization approach can lead to significant cost reductions (e.g., 7.8% in the case study) compared to scenarios with fixed power limits and no port energy management.
*   **Contribution:** The paper addresses a gap in the literature by providing a comprehensive methodology for simultaneous optimization of large-capacity, high-speed ferry operations and charging infrastructure design with global optimality guarantees.

structure.title: METHODOLOGY
structure.summary: This partial document focuses on the methodology for optimizing vessel operations and energy systems. It defines the problem by introducing sets of vessels and ports, along with their characteristics like distance, battery size, weight, and friction constants. The planning horizon is discretized into time periods. The document then details the decision variables, which include the state of energy in stationary storage at each site, power flow to and from the grid, PV generation, vessel battery state of energy, and charging power from sites to vessels. The constraints are categorized into vessel operational constraints and shore-side constraints. Vessel operational constraints cover earliest and latest departure/arrival times, travel time determined by speed and distance, energy consumption per leg (with a linear approximation for a convex envelope), and linking energy charged to charging decisions. It also enforces depth-of-discharge limits, maximum energy constraints, and periodic constraints for the start and end of trips. Charging is restricted to when vessels are moored, and the charging power is defined as the sum of power from the grid, PV, and battery, with an indicator variable for vessel location. Finally, it defines the net energy charged for a vessel/leg combination.

nodes.title: Vessel Operation Constraints
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a methodology for optimizing the joint infrastructure and energy management of a ferry service. The core of the methodology involves a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation that considers various decision variables and constraints related to vessel operations, port-side energy systems, and costs.

Key aspects covered include:

*   **Vessel Operations:** Defining vessel characteristics (battery size, weight, friction), itineraries with legs, and time windows for departure and arrival. It also models vessel energy consumption, charging power, and state of charge constraints, including depth-of-discharge and maximum energy limits.
*   **Port-Side Energy Systems:** Describing local energy systems at each port, including peak grid connection, photovoltaic (PV) generation capacity, and stationary energy storage. It defines decision variables for these systems, such as storage state of energy, net power, grid power flow, and PV production.
*   **Constraints:** Establishing operational constraints for both vessels and shore-side systems. This includes time window adherence, speed-distance relationships, energy consumption modeling, battery charge/discharge limits, and ensuring charging occurs only when vessels are moored. Port-side constraints cover power delivery limits, grid interaction, PV generation limits, and stationary battery dynamics.
*   **Costs and Objective Function:** Defining various cost components, including capital expenses for stationary storage, PV generation, grid connections, and vessel batteries, as well as operational costs related to electricity purchase and sale. The objective is to minimize the total cost.
*   **Problem Formulation:** Presenting the overall optimization problem as a MILP, which can be solved to optimality.
*   **Case Study:** Describing a specific case study involving the China Zorrilla ferry operating between Buenos Aires and Colonia del Sacramento. It outlines the vessel specifications, charging infrastructure, service frequency, and energy prices used in the analysis.
*   **Results:** Presenting numerical results from four different experimental scenarios, comparing designs with and without local energy management systems, PV generation, stationary batteries, and optimized vessel battery design. The results highlight cost reductions achieved through the integration of these technologies.
*   **Discussion:** Offering comments on model assumptions, limitations regarding MILP scalability for large fleets, and potential extensions such as Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) services.

structure.title: CASESTUDY
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses an optimization algorithm for ferry operations, specifically focusing on the China Zorrilla ferry route between Buenos Aires and Colonia del Sacramento. The main points covered are:

*   **Case Study Setup:** Detailed input parameters and experimental design for testing the optimization algorithm. This includes specifications for the China Zorrilla ferry (capacity, dimensions, battery size, speed, charging infrastructure), service frequency, and historical data for solar power generation and energy prices in Buenos Aires and Colonia.
*   **Optimization Model and Solver:** The use of Yalmip for formulating the optimization problem and Gurobi as the solver, along with the computational resources and time required.
*   **Experimental Scenarios:** Four experiments are described, progressively introducing elements like PV generation, optimized peak power, stationary batteries, and optimized vessel battery design.
*   **Results and Analysis:** A summary of the results from the four experiments, including the resulting designs and associated costs. Experiment 1 (current design) is presented as the baseline with the highest cost, while subsequent experiments show cost reductions achieved through the introduction of PV systems and other optimizations. The document also mentions figures that will detail vessel and shore-side results.
*   **Discussion of Limitations and Future Work:** The authors acknowledge simplifications made in the study, such as assuming slight variations in vessel displacement with battery configuration. They also highlight the limitations of MILP scalability for large fleets and suggest future research directions, including decomposition methods and exploring Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) services.

nodes.title: Designs and Costs
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes a case study for optimizing the economic viability of electric ferry services, specifically focusing on the China Zorrilla ferry route between Buenos Aires and Colonia del Sacramento. The main points covered are:

*   **Case Study Setup:** Details the specific parameters for the China Zorrilla ferry, including passenger/vehicle capacity, dimensions, battery capacity, motor specifications, charging infrastructure, service frequency, and the route. It also outlines the data sources for solar power generation and energy prices.
*   **Optimization Experiments:** Presents four experiments designed to test the optimization algorithm:
    *   Experiment 1: Baseline scenario with no local energy management (EMS) or PV generation.
    *   Experiment 2: Includes PV generation at each port.
    *   Experiment 3: Adds a stationary battery system in addition to PV.
    *   Experiment 4: Optimizes vessel battery design alongside PV and stationary batteries, achieving the lowest total cost.
*   **Results and Analysis:**
    *   **Designs and Costs:** Compares the total costs for each experiment, showing significant cost reductions with the inclusion of PV, stationary batteries, and optimized vessel batteries. Experiment 4 yielded the lowest total cost.
    *   **Vessel Results:** Illustrates the energy state and power exchanges for the vessels in Experiment 4, highlighting charging patterns during mooring periods and the primary power sources (grid, with smaller contributions from onboard batteries and PV).
    *   **Port Side Results:** Details the energy and power dynamics at the ports in Experiment 4, emphasizing the dominance of grid power for vessel charging, the supporting role of stationary batteries, and the limited contribution of PV.
*   **Discussion:** Addresses limitations and future research directions, including the assumption of slight vessel displacement variation, the scalability of the MILP model for larger fleets, and the potential for incorporating Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) services.
*   **Conclusion:** Summarizes the effectiveness of the proposed optimization framework in reducing total costs (capital and operational) by 7.8% compared to an unoptimized scenario. It highlights the framework's utility for both design planning and weekly scheduling. Future work will focus on incorporating power consumption variability, stochastic forecasts, and battery degradation.

structure.title: CONCLUSION
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a system configuration for experiments related to electric ship services, focusing on optimizing costs through various infrastructure and energy storage combinations.

The main points covered are:

*   **Experimental Setup:** Table II outlines four different experimental configurations (Exp. 1-4) with varying parameters such as PV generation capacity (Ppv), battery energy capacity (Eb,i), charging power (Ppv,i), and associated costs (C-energy, C+energy, Ctot).
*   **Experiment Progression:** The experiments demonstrate a progressive inclusion of components:
    *   Experiment 1: Baseline project design.
    *   Experiment 2: PV generation only.
    *   Experiment 3: PV system and a stationary battery.
    *   Experiment 4: PV system, stationary battery, and an optimized vessel battery.
*   **Cost Analysis:** The document highlights how the inclusion of stationary and optimized vessel batteries leads to significant reductions in total weekly costs, with Experiment 4 achieving the lowest total cost.
*   **Operational Aspects:** Figures 3 and 4 illustrate vessel and port-side energy and power dynamics, respectively, for Experiment 4. Key observations include:
    *   Vessels primarily charge from the grid during mooring periods, with battery and PV contributions being smaller.
    *   The grid is the dominant power source for vessel charging at ports, with batteries also playing a supporting role.
    *   PV generation is limited and mainly utilized during daylight hours.
    *   Grid-to-battery and battery-to-grid flows are less frequent, suggesting the battery's primary role is local support rather than energy arbitrage.
*   **Optimization Framework:** The paper presents an optimization framework that jointly optimizes charging schedules, infrastructure investments, and speed profiles to improve economic viability.
*   **Results and Conclusion:** The proposed framework reduces total costs by 7.8% compared to an unoptimized scenario. The conclusion emphasizes the potential of advanced optimization techniques for improving upfront and total cost metrics for electric ship services.
*   **Future Work:** Planned future research includes incorporating power consumption variability, stochastic forecasts for weather and prices, and a more detailed treatment of battery degradation.
*   **Acknowledgments and References:** The document includes acknowledgments for contributions and a comprehensive list of references related to electric ship technology, energy storage, and optimization.
